title: No beginning to find
hook: count your mothers with twigs, your fathers with balls of clay, and the earth runs out first (SN 15.1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tears and the four oceans, and your line, be gentle with grief. Were you gentle with someone's grief? Today the same chapter opens, with grass and clay and a counting game no one can finish. Day six hundred fifty.

Family trees are popular. You can send off a sample of your spit and get back a map of where your great-great-grandparents lived. Go back far enough, though, and the branches multiply faster than anyone can count. Two parents, four grandparents, eight, sixteen, and soon the chart is wider than the page. The Buddha starts the chapter on the long round of lives with a family tree too. But instead of paper, he uses all the grass in India, and then the whole earth. Today: anamatagga.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE BY MAIL.` → `TWO, FOUR, EIGHT, SIXTEEN.` → `NOW USE ALL THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: SN 15.1 opens the chapter with a sentence the rest of the chapter keeps returning to. This round of wandering, monks, is without a discoverable beginning. No first point can be found where beings, blocked by not knowing and tied by craving, started roaming. Then the picture. Suppose someone cut all the grass, sticks, branches and leaves in all of India, gathered them in one heap, and cut them into little sticks, each four fingers long. Then, laying them down one at a time, they counted: this is my mother, this is my mother's mother, and on and on. The grass and sticks of India would run out before the line of mothers did. SN 15.2 does the same with the earth. Roll the whole earth into balls of clay the size of a jujube seed, and put them down: this is my father, this is my father's father. The earth runs out first. Then the same conclusion: for so long you have experienced loss and suffering. It's enough to grow weary of all this, and to be free. The images are meant to stretch the mind until it gives up trying to find the edge. Not a large number; no number at all. No beginning to find. A little later in the same chapter, the Buddha draws out one surprising consequence. It is hard, he says, to find a being who has not at some time been your mother, or your father, your brother, sister, son or daughter. Some Buddhist teachers, in Tibet especially, have built a practice of kindness on that line: anyone you meet may once have been family.
screen: `WITHOUT A DISCOVERABLE BEGINNING` · `GRASS AND STICKS: MY MOTHER'S MOTHER` · `BALLS OF CLAY: MY FATHER'S FATHER` · `ANYONE MAY ONCE HAVE BEEN FAMILY` · then, large: `NO BEGINNING TO FIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone you'll see today who isn't family. A coworker, a cashier, a neighbor, someone you find difficult. Picture them clearly. Then, gently, try the old thought: at some time, in some way, this one may have been my mother, my father, my brother or sister. You don't have to believe it as a fact to let it change how they look. Notice any softening. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.

anamatagga. The Pali word for 'without a discoverable beginning,' describing the round of lives in SN 15.1-15.2: the grass of India and the clay of the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers does. Today's word.
Your line: anyone may have been family. Treat one person today as you would family, with a little more patience than they'd expect. Day six hundred fifty.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism especially, students practice recognizing all beings as having once been their mothers, as a basis for compassion; teachers in other traditions draw on the same chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya.

fork.setup: you're cutting all the grass of India into little sticks, one for each mother back through your line. what happens?
options: the line of mothers and the grass end together.
fork.reveal: the grass runs out, and the line of mothers goes on: the round has no beginning to find.

original.note: Pali anamatagga: without a discoverable beginning. SN 15 is the Anamatagga Samyutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: no beginning to find means the past is long.
what it means: in SN 15.1–2, the round of lives has no discoverable beginning; the grass and the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers.

what a scholar hears: anamatagga is rendered 'whose first point is not known'; the same chapter's line that it is hard to find a being who has not been one's mother is echoed in Tibetan practices for developing compassion.

notes: SN 15.1–2 paraphrased. Confirm: grass, sticks, branches and foliage of Jambudipa, cut into pieces four fingers long, laid down 'this is my mother, this my mother's mother'; earth made into balls the size of jujube kernels for fathers.
'The next twenty discourses' assumes SN 15 has about twenty suttas; please check the count.
SN 15.14–19: it is not easy to find a being who has not been one's mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter; confirm the references.
The Tibetan practice of recognizing all beings as mothers (part of the seven-point cause and effect instruction) is described generally; confirm the link drawn to this chapter is fair.
The hook's mail-in DNA test is a modern image, not a claim.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'the next twenty discourses' was off (SN 15 has twenty suttas in all, so nineteen follow) and is now 'the rest of the chapter'; 'many teachers' softened; the trapdoor no longer says the chapter 'became the root' of Tibetan practice and no longer overstates the sutta as 'all beings have been our mothers'.
